newsitem.title: UK: Tax experts say UK dividend tax aimed at banks.
newsitem.headline: Tax experts say UK dividend tax aimed at banks.

text.p: Arbitrage trades and lending in the form of preference shares are the two main targets of a British budget measure taxing share dividends which are trading assets, tax experts said on Thursday.
The change, announced in Wednesday's budget, will affect investment banks which provide loans and firms which buy shares to try to generate tax-free interest, they added.

A number of major investment banks in London were not immediately able to comment on how they would be affected by the change, which Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said in his first budget should yield nearly 500 million stg in the period to April 2001.
Some doubted, however, if the measure would generate this much over the period.
The change, whereby "dividends on shares which are trading assets will themselves be treated as part of the holder's trading profits", came into effect immediately.
A tax expert at one major accountancy firm said the measure would hit dealers used to buying shares when the dividend was due to be paid and then selling them.

But the budget stressed those who hold shares as investments would not be affected by the measure, which supersedes previous rules under which only certain dividends on such shares were treated as part of the trading profits.
It said the measures meant dividends on UK equities could, on the whole, be taken outside the scope of the provision.
"Changes have been made so that in future this provision will apply mainly to transactions in overseas equities by dealers," it added.
But the government also warned firms against taking measures to avoid the tax.

"If the government has reason to think that this yield is being reduced by moving shares into the hands of associates for whom they are not trading assets, it will take action to block such manoeuvres," it said.
Any such action would take effect from the introduction of the new rules, it added.
